caption: Figure 1: Many problems in image processing, graphics, and vision involve translating an input image into a corresponding output image. These problems are often treated with application-specific algorithms, even though the setting is always the same: map pixels to pixels. Conditional adversarial nets are a general-purpose solution that appears to work well on a wide variety of these problems. Here we show results of the method on several. In each case we use the same architecture and objective, and simply train on different data.
description:
Figure type: Image collage showing various image-to-image translation tasks.
Description: The figure displays multiple image translation tasks using conditional adversarial networks. Each task includes an input image and its corresponding output image. Tasks include translating labels to street scenes, facades, black-and-white to color, aerial images to maps, day to night, and edges to photos.

Text in figure: Labels to Street Scene, Labels to Facade, BW to Color, Aerial to Map, Day to Night, Edges to Photo, input, output.

caption: Figure 2: Training a conditional GAN to map edges → photo. The discriminator, D , learns to classify between fake (synthesized by the generator) and real { edge, photo } tuples. The generator, G , learns to fool the discriminator. Unlike an unconditional GAN, both the generator and discriminator observe the input edge map.
description:
Figure: A diagram showing the training of a conditional GAN for image-to-image translation.
Shows two processes: one for generating fake images and another for classifying real images.
Contains two main components: a generator (G) and a discriminator (D).
The generator takes an input image (x) and produces a fake image (G(x)).
The discriminator takes a pair of images (edge, photo) and classifies them as real or fake.
The discriminator also receives the input image (x) to help in classification.

Text in figure: G, D, x, G(x), fake, real, edge, photo.

caption: Figure 3: Two choices for the architecture of the generator. The 'U-Net' [50] is an encoder-decoder with skip connections between mirrored layers in the encoder and decoder stacks.
description:
Section 1: Figure type and content
This figure is a schematic diagram comparing two architectures for a generator in image-to-image translation. It shows an Encoder-Decoder architecture on the left and a U-Net architecture on the right. Both architectures take an input x and produce an output y. The Encoder-Decoder has a simple linear flow from input to output, while the U-Net includes skip connections between mirrored layers in the encoder and decoder stacks.

Section 2: Figure details
Text in figure: "Encoder-decoder", "U-Net", "x", "y".
Blocks and layers: Encoder-Decoder has two blocks connected in series; U-Net has multiple blocks with skip connections. Arrows indicate the flow of data from input x to output y.

caption: Figure 4: Different losses induce different quality of results. Each column shows results trained under a different loss. Please see https://phillipi.github.io/pix2pix/ for additional examples.

caption: Figure 9: Colorization results of conditional GANs versus the L2 regression from [62] and the full method (classification with rebalancing) from [64]. The cGANs can produce compelling colorizations (first two rows), but have a common failure mode of producing a grayscale or desaturated result (last row).
description:
Description: The figure displays a comparison of colorization results from different methods. It shows images of a coffee maker, a bird, and a fox, each processed by four different methods: L2 regression, classification with rebalancing, conditional GANs, and ground truth. The conditional GANs produce visually appealing colorizations but sometimes result in grayscale or desaturated images.

Text in figure: L2 [62], Classification (rebal.) [62], Ours (L1 + cGAN), Ground truth

caption: Figure 10: Applying a conditional GAN to semantic segmentation. The cGAN produces sharp images that look at glance like the ground truth, but in fact include many small, hallucinated objects.
description:

Text in Figure: Input, Ground truth, L1, cGAN.
